extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific investigation; readers of philosophy of science and methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and evaluating methodological criteria for investigating complex phenomena (induction, experiment, deduction, verification) as presented in a philosophy-of-science/textbook treatment. Emphasis on when methods succeed or fail and on the precautions needed in experimentation and theory-testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of simple observation / Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of simple observation (comparing recovered cases to see if they were preceded by the administration of an agent) is inapplicable to intricate cases where many causes concur; it yields at best a vague general impression of efficacy unless the association is absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 'plurality of causes' ensures many recoveries will occur without the agent and many failures with it, instances of recovery/failure will not reliably agree in the administration or non-administration of the agent. Only when all (or essentially all) recoveries coincide with the agent could simple observation support confident generalization. Example: using hospital returns might show only a slight excess of recoveries with mercury—of very secondary value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/Experimental method must be strictly empirical
rubrics_metrics.description: The experimental method, when applied to a complex case, must be 'completely, not incompletely, empirical'—i.e., experiments should be made directly upon the complex case rather than by deducing from experiments on simpler or healthy cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If experiments on simpler cases (e.g., mercury on a healthy person) are used together with deduction to predict effects on diseased persons, that is deduction not pure experiment. For the method to be empirical it must seek a direct answer to the specific complex question: 'Does or does not mercury tend to cure the particular disease?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertainment of experimental circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: When devising an experiment to ascertain the effect of an agent, introduce it into circumstances which have been exactly ascertained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In life-phenomena this is rarely realized because we do not know all pre-existing circumstances in any instance; the difficulty can be mitigated by multiplying experiments in varied circumstances to make it improbable that unknown causes exist in them all. Still, lack of exact ascertainment severely limits experimental conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude or allow for confounding causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure none of the known circumstances have effects susceptible of being confounded with those of the agent under study, or arrange them so that their influence can be computed and subtracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take utmost pains to exclude causes capable of composition with the given cause; if any are present, make them such that their effect can be calculated and allowed for, so the residual phenomenon reveals the agent's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication of experiments to dilute unknown causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a sufficient multiplicity of experiments in diverse circumstances so that unknown causes are unlikely to be present in all of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeating experiments across varied settings may attenuate the obstacle posed by unknown concurrent causes, though it will not always suffice in complex biological or social phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inapplicability of the Method of Difference in complex intermixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary Method of Difference (comparing the state following an experiment with the state preceding it) is unavailing when multiple influences operate during the transition; comparing different cases (identical except in one respect) is often chimerical in complex phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In complicated phenomena one cannot be sure two cases are similar in all respects but one, so both modes of the Method of Difference fail to isolate causal effects reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental results in conjunct effects often only show tendency frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: In effects resulting from the union of many causes, experiments generally can only show that a cause is very often followed by an effect, not measure its share; only very potent causes produce sufficiently large proportions of success to be regarded as experimental truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of 'Specifics' sufficiently proved by direct experiment include quinine, colchicum, lime-juice, cod-liver oil. Even these do not always work, but succeed in a large enough proportion to be experimental truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsuitability of experimental method for politics and history
rubrics_metrics.description: The experimental/observational approach is even less applicable to political and historical phenomena due to extreme plurality of causes, inextricable interweaving of effects, and the impossibility of making identical or controlled experiments on nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent inductive arguments from individual instances (e.g., 'an institution is good because a country prospered with it') ignore plurality of causes. Even deliberate policy changes cannot be cleanly isolated since many other influencing circumstances change before effects become inductively assessable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive Method structure: Induction, Ratiocination, Verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deductive Method consists of three operations: (1) a direct induction to obtain laws of the individual causes; (2) ratiocination to determine the combined effect from those laws; (3) verification by comparison with observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction provides premises (laws of separate causes); ratiocination combines them (often requiring mathematics); verification tests deductive conclusions against empirical results and is essential to render deductions reliable rather than conjectural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive foundation: ascertain laws of each separate cause
rubrics_metrics.description: First requisite of the Deductive Method is to know the laws of the different tendencies (each concurrent cause); these laws must be obtained by direct observation or experiment on each cause separately, or by prior deduction ultimately grounded in induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To apply deduction to social or physical phenomena one must investigate or suppose known the laws of human action or mechanical/chemical/vital laws respectively. If the causes cannot be separated for study, the inductive foundation is uncertain and weakens subsequent deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer cases where a tendency operates alone for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of a tendency should, if possible, be studied in cases where that tendency operates alone or only with agencies whose effects are known/calculable; avoid inferring laws from cases in which the tendency is counteracted or substantially modified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studying tendencies from cases where they are mixed with other unknown influences hampers discovery of their laws (e.g., laws of motion could not be found from observations of bodies kept at rest by equilibrium). When separation is impossible, use Method of Concomitant Variations when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pathological/natural experiments in physiology when direct separation impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathological facts (localized disease disturbances) often serve as valuable equivalents to controlled experiments for physiological investigation, provided early stages and locality are known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artificially produced pathological facts (e.g., nerve section) and experiments on healthy organisms can better isolate laws; select cases whose circumstances can be best ascertained—usually health rather than disease—because disease is changeable and introduces unpredictable agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratiocination requirement: computation from laws of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The second stage is a process of calculation or ratiocination: determining from the laws of the causes what effect any given combination will produce, often requiring numerical/geometrical/theoretical apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where laws are sufficiently precise, mathematical theorems are used (e.g., calculus in celestial mechanics); but complexity may preclude exact solutions, limiting deduction to approximate results or to qualitative inference from general laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification as essential test of deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductions must be verified by careful comparison with direct observation wherever available; verification is the test that guards against errors in omitted causes or incorrect numerical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If observed cases contradict deductions, one must explain what frustrated the deduction; verification should include cases at least as complex as those for which the theory will be applied. A true theory is expected to lead deductively to known empirical laws (e.g., Newtonian theory leading to Kepler's laws).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of empirical laws and comprehensive description for verification
rubrics_metrics.description: To facilitate verification, ascertain as many empirical laws as possible (by Method of Agreement) and describe phenomena comprehensively and accurately, expressing wholes in terms of simplest correct expressions obtained from parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical uniformities (even partial) and detailed phenomenon descriptions make it easier to check whether a deductive theory accounts for observed regularities; expressing observed series in progressively accurate forms (circle → epicycles → ellipse) is illustrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex cases become evidence when explained by theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex instances which could not aid discovery may, once a law is deduced otherwise, serve as new experiments confirming the law when the law explains those complex cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A law gains certainty by explaining complex cases not previously considered, and such confirmations can also help reveal previously unexcluded circumstances. Example: discrepancy in velocity of sound explained by heat from condensation confirmed law of heat development by compression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to account for failures of deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: When a deduction predicts an effect for a given combination of causes, in known instances where the combination existed but the effect did not occur, the theory must show (or plausibly surmise) what frustrated it; otherwise the theory is imperfect and unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification is incomplete unless such explanations for discrepancies can be supplied; mere failure to predict demands modification or rejection of the deductive theory until explained.
